issues.legal_issue: A High Court exercising writ jurisdiction may not re-examine concurrent factual findings of revenue authorities in the absence of an error of law.
material_facts: Revenue authorities successively upheld the surplus-area determination, finding that the cultivation records relied on to establish the sons’ tenancy had been tampered with and that the claims concerning other land were unsupported.
The authorities found no evidence that the sons paid rent or that an agreement relieved them of rent, and found no proof that the land claimed as uncultivated land qualified for exclusion.
The High Court dismissed the writ petition challenging the revenue orders.
issues.conclusion: The revenue orders disclosed no error of law warranting interference, and the High Court was justified in dismissing the writ petition in limine.
issues.legal_principle: In a proceeding under Article 226 of the Constitution, the High Court does not exercise appellate jurisdiction and cannot re-examine or disturb a tribunal’s findings of fact in the absence of an error of law.

rule.if: constitutional_writ_proceeding and concurrent_factual_findings and not error_of_law_in_orders

predicates.constitutional_writ_proceeding: A party challenged an inferior court’s or tribunal’s decision by seeking constitutional writ relief.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: More than one lower authority reached the same findings of fact.
predicates.error_of_law_in_orders: The challenged orders contain an error of law.

issues.definition: When a constitutional writ proceeding challenges concurrent factual findings and the orders contain no error of law, interference is unwarranted.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may receive additional evidence only under a judicial, limited discretion, and should refuse it when it can decide the appeal on the existing material.
material_facts: The appellants applied to introduce additional documents and testimony in the appeal.
The Court was able to decide the appeal on the material already before it and found no inherent lacuna or obscurity requiring further evidence.
The Court considered that the application sought to fill gaps using revenue records that lower authorities had found spurious.
issues.conclusion: The application to adduce additional evidence was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: Order 41, Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure confines the appellate court’s discretion to admit additional evidence; the test is whether the court can pronounce judgment on the existing materials without the proposed evidence. The Court relied on Arjun Singh alias Puran v. Kartar Singh.

predicates.appellate_proceeding: A court is considering a matter in its appellate capacity.
predicates.additional_evidence_application: A party applies to introduce evidence that was not part of the existing record.
predicates.existing_record_sufficient: The court can decide the matter on the materials already before it without the proposed evidence.

issues.definition: In an appellate proceeding, an application for additional evidence is refused when the existing record is sufficient for the court to decide the matter.

issues.legal_issue: A claim to exclude land from a surplus-area determination as tenants’ permissible area or as uncultivated land requires supporting evidence of the relevant tenancy or land-use facts.
material_facts: The sons claimed that they had cultivated certain land as tenants before the relevant law commenced, but the authorities found the cultivation entries relied on for that claim to have been tampered with.
The record did not show that the sons paid rent or that an agreement relieved them of the obligation to pay rent.

The landowner claimed that certain land was uncultivated land to be excluded, but the authorities found no proof that it was not being used for an agricultural or agriculture-related purpose or for pasture at the relevant time.
issues.conclusion: The claimed tenancy and uncultivated-land exclusions were not established and did not warrant disturbing the surplus-area determination.
issues.legal_principle: Under the Punjab Tenancy Act, 1887, the Court considered the absence of rent or evidence of an agreement relieving the alleged tenants from rent in assessing the tenancy claim. Under section 2(8) of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, a landowner claiming exclusion of banjar qadim or banjar jadid land had to prove that, at the relevant time, it was not used for an agricultural purpose, a purpose subservient to agriculture, or pasture.

rule.if: surplus_area_determination and tenancy_exclusion_claim and unreliable_cultivation_records and no_rent_or_rent_exemption_evidence and uncultivated_land_exclusion_claim and no_proof_of_nonagricultural_use

predicates.surplus_area_determination: An authority is determining which land is surplus for the purposes of a land-tenure regime.
predicates.tenancy_exclusion_claim: A party claims that land should be excluded because it was held or cultivated as tenants’ permissible area.
predicates.unreliable_cultivation_records: The records relied on to establish cultivation are found unreliable or tampered with.
predicates.no_rent_or_rent_exemption_evidence: There is no evidence of rent paid or of an agreement relieving the alleged tenants from rent.
predicates.uncultivated_land_exclusion_claim: A landowner claims that land should be excluded as uncultivated land.
predicates.no_proof_of_nonagricultural_use: There is no proof that the land was not used for agriculture, a purpose subservient to agriculture, or pasture at the relevant time.

issues.definition: In a surplus-area determination, the claimed exclusions are unestablished when the tenancy claim rests on unreliable records without evidence of rent or exemption, and the landowner provides no proof supporting the claimed uncultivated-land status.
